title: HIS-201 Ch. 3 — 3 Numbers & Dates
subject: HIS-201
topic: Chapter 3: Colonization and Conflict in the South

cards.term: When Juan de Oñate founded New Mexico
cards.def: In 1598 Juan de Oñate led colonists, soldiers, and slaves to the upper Rio Grande, founding Spain's lasting colony of New Mexico.

cards.term: When Santa Fe was founded
cards.def: In 1610 the Spanish founded Santa Fe, the second-oldest European town in the present-day United States after St. Augustine.

cards.term: How many colonists lived in New Mexico by 1675
cards.def: By 1675 New Mexico held only about 2,500 Spanish colonists, showing how unattractive the poor northern outpost was to settlers.

cards.term: How large Florida's mission network was by 1675
cards.def: By 1675 forty Franciscan missions in Florida served as many as 26,000 baptized Indians, extending Spain's reach beyond St. Augustine.

cards.term: When the Pueblo Revolt began
cards.def: On August 10, 1680, the Pueblo Indians rose against Spanish rule, killed colonists, besieged Santa Fe, and drove the survivors south.

cards.term: When Spain reconquered New Mexico
cards.def: In 1692, about a dozen years after the Pueblo Revolt, Spain returned and reconquered New Mexico.

cards.term: When the Virginia Company received its charter
cards.def: In 1606 James I chartered the Virginia Company of London as a private venture to colonize the Chesapeake.

cards.term: When Jamestown was founded
cards.def: In the spring of 1607 the Virginia Company's 100 men and four boys founded Jamestown on Powhatan's territory, beginning England's permanent colonization.

cards.term: When the starving time struck Jamestown
cards.def: In the winter of 1609 to 1610 disease, salt-poisoned water, hunger, and conflict left only about sixty Jamestown settlers alive.

cards.term: When Pocahontas married John Rolfe
cards.def: In 1614 Pocahontas married John Rolfe, and Powhatan used the alliance to gain English weapons and labor against rival Indians.

cards.term: When Powhatan still ruled a flourishing confederacy
cards.def: In 1617 Powhatan still ruled a thriving Chesapeake confederacy, though English tobacco fields were beginning to change the balance of power.

cards.term: When the House of Burgesses first met
cards.def: In 1619 Virginia's House of Burgesses first met, creating the first representative assembly in England's American colonies.

cards.term: When the Powhatans launched their great attack
cards.def: In March 1622 Opechancanough's coordinated attack killed about one-quarter of Virginia's colonists, provoking devastating English retaliation.

cards.term: When Virginia became a royal colony
cards.def: In 1624 James I dissolved the Virginia Company and made Virginia a royal colony under direct Crown rule.

cards.term: When Maryland was founded
cards.def: In 1632 the Calvert family received Maryland as a proprietary colony, a Catholic-led settlement that tolerated all Christians.

cards.term: When Maryland's tobacco rivalry sparked another Indian war
cards.def: In 1644 a second major war broke out between the Chesapeake Indians and the English, fueled by the spread of Maryland's and Virginia's tobacco plantations.

cards.term: How many colonists Virginia had by 1650
cards.def: By 1650 Virginia had stabilized and could claim about 15,000 colonists despite decades of disease and Indian war.

cards.term: When England's civil war and restoration changed colonial policy
cards.def: After Charles I's execution in 1649 and the restoration of the monarchy in 1660, Charles II demanded that the colonies contribute more to English prosperity.

cards.term: When the first Navigation Act was passed
cards.def: In 1660 Parliament passed the first of the Navigation Acts, reserving colonial shipping for England and limiting enumerated exports to English ports.

cards.term: When later Navigation Acts tightened trade
cards.def: In 1663 and 1673 Parliament added Navigation Acts that routed colonial imports through England and imposed duties on colonial trade.

cards.term: When Bacon's Rebellion occurred
cards.def: In 1676 Nathaniel Bacon's followers attacked Indians, fought Governor Berkeley's supporters, and burned Jamestown before Bacon's death ended the revolt.

cards.term: When Coode's Rebellion occurred
cards.def: In July 1689 John Coode's rebels overthrew Maryland's proprietary government, and England revoked the Calverts' charter until 1715.

cards.term: When the Royal African Company lost its monopoly
cards.def: In 1698 the Royal African Company lost its monopoly on the English slave trade, and competing merchants sharply increased African imports.

cards.term: When North Carolina became a separate colony
cards.def: In 1701, about forty years after the Carolina grant, North Carolina became a separate colony, becoming a poor colony of small farms and naval stores separate from South Carolina.

cards.term: When the Yamasee War occurred
cards.def: In 1715 the Yamasees attacked South Carolina, nearly destroying the colony and ending the region's Indian slave trade and its proprietary rule.

cards.term: When South Carolina became a royal colony
cards.def: In 1729 the Crown formally made South Carolina a royal colony, and rice exports soon restored its prosperity.

cards.term: When Georgia was chartered
cards.def: In 1732 George II gave Georgia's trustees a twenty-one-year charter for a buffer against Spanish Florida and a refuge for the worthy poor.

cards.term: When Georgia became a royal colony
cards.def: In 1752 Georgia passed to royal control after the trustees had abandoned their limits on land, slavery, and liquor.

cards.term: How much Oñate's backers expected to recoup
cards.def: Juan de Oñate and his backers expected colonizing New Mexico to repay more than half a million pesos, but they found little mineral wealth.

cards.term: How many people Oñate led to New Mexico in 1598
cards.def: In 1598 Juan de Oñate led 500 colonists, soldiers, and slaves to the upper Rio Grande, finding modest villages, no ocean, and little mineral wealth.

cards.term: How many Acoma people the Spanish killed
cards.def: Vicente de Zaldívar's punitive expedition killed perhaps 800 Acoma people and enslaved several hundred, and Oñate ordered surviving adult males to lose one foot.

cards.term: When royal authorities removed Oñate
cards.def: In 1606 royal authorities removed Juan de Oñate as New Mexico's governor for mismanagement and abuse of Indians.

cards.term: What reward the Crown promised New Mexico settlers
cards.def: The Spanish Crown promised New Mexico settlers minor nobility after five years, yet many still abandoned the arid colony.

cards.term: How many people St. Augustine had in 1600 and 1675
cards.def: St. Augustine survived with about 500 people in 1600 and reached about 1,500 by the bishop's tour in 1675.

cards.term: How many Pueblo households held captives by 1680
cards.def: By 1680 half of New Mexican Spanish households held at least one Indian captive taken through war, purchase, or slave raids.

cards.term: What annual tribute each Pueblo household owed
cards.def: Each Pueblo household officially owed Spain three bushels of corn and one processed hide or large cotton blanket every year, plus public labor.

cards.term: How much smallpox reduced the Pueblo population
cards.def: Smallpox arrived in the early 1620s and cut the Pueblo population by 70 percent to about 30,000 in less than a generation.

cards.term: How many Pueblo villages remained by 1680
cards.def: Pueblo villages fell from roughly 100 at contact to only 30 inhabited villages in 1680.

cards.term: How Spain punished Pueblo religious leaders in the 1670s
cards.def: Spanish authorities arrested Pueblo religious leaders, executed two, and publicly whipped forty-three, including Popé, before the Pueblo Revolt.

cards.term: How many colonists founded Jamestown
cards.def: In 1607, 104 colonists, 100 men and four boys, arrived in three ships, and the first two English women reached Jamestown in fall 1608.

cards.term: When John Smith left Jamestown
cards.def: In 1609 Captain John Smith returned to England after an accidental gunpowder injury, ending his brief imposition of order at Jamestown.

cards.term: How long Virginia Company laborers served
cards.def: Virginia Company laborers served seven years in exchange for passage, and later indenture promoters promised land and wealth after four to seven years.

cards.term: When the headright system began and what it granted
cards.def: In 1618 the Virginia Company's headright system gave existing colonists 100 acres, new settlers 50 acres, and sponsors 50 acres per immigrant whose passage they paid.

cards.term: How many immigrants entered the Chesapeake in the 1620s
cards.def: In the 1620s 130,000 to 150,000 immigrants, mostly aged fifteen to twenty-four, entered the Chesapeake, and men outnumbered women six to one.

cards.term: What share of Virginia immigrants were indentured servants
cards.def: Indentured servants made up three-quarters of Virginia immigrants, and about 40 percent of servants did not survive their terms.

cards.term: What Chesapeake life expectancy was
cards.def: A Chesapeake man who reached age twenty could expect to live only to forty-eight, and women's life expectancy was even lower.

cards.term: How many immigrants died before the Virginia Company was dissolved
cards.def: More than 3,000 immigrants died in Chesapeake conditions before James I dissolved the Virginia Company in 1624.

cards.term: How Chesapeake child mortality affected families
cards.def: One in four Chesapeake children died before maturity, and among those reaching eighteen, one-third had lost both parents.

cards.term: How much land the Calverts controlled
cards.def: The Calvert family controlled ten million acres of Maryland, along with its justice and civil government, after founding the colony in 1632.

cards.term: How many people lived in Maryland by 1640
cards.def: By 1640 about 2,000 Maryland inhabitants planted tobacco on land that Virginians wanted, renewing tension with the Indians.

cards.term: How Opechancanough's 1644 attack ended
cards.def: In 1644 Opechancanough killed hundreds of colonists and halted the frontier, but he was captured and shot and the Powhatan confederacy ended.

cards.term: How many Virginia free white men were landless by 1676
cards.def: By 1676 one-quarter of Virginia's free white men were landless, as tobacco overproduction and Navigation duties crushed small planters.

cards.term: When Bacon burned Jamestown
cards.def: In September 1676 Nathaniel Bacon burned Jamestown and died of dysentery a month later, ending Bacon's Rebellion.

cards.term: What share of Chesapeake inhabitants were Black in 1675
cards.def: Black people made up only 5 percent of Chesapeake inhabitants in 1675, when planters still preferred English indentured servants.

cards.term: When Africans first arrived in Virginia
cards.def: Africans arrived in Virginia by 1619, probably through Dutch traders, and some early Black settlers were English-speaking Christians, servants, or free.

cards.term: How many Africans British dealers sold annually after 1698
cards.def: After the Royal African Company's monopoly ended in 1698, British dealers sold 20,000 Africans annually.

cards.term: How enslaved Africans compared with European migrants, 1492 to 1820
cards.def: From 1492 to 1820 enslaved Africans arriving in the Americas outnumbered European migrants almost five to one.

cards.term: How annual slave imports grew before and after sugar
cards.def: Slave imports to the Americas were a few thousand yearly before 1600, then rose to 19,000 yearly in the seventeenth century and 60,000 yearly in the eighteenth.

cards.term: How many Africans were captured between 1700 and 1850
cards.def: Between 1700 and 1850 as many as 21 million West Africans were captured, about 9 million entered the Americas, and as many as 7 million remained enslaved in Africa.

cards.term: Where nine-tenths of enslaved Africans landed
cards.def: Nine-tenths of Africans taken to the New World landed in Brazil or the Caribbean islands, and only about 4 percent went to North America.

cards.term: What share of new Chesapeake slaves came directly from Africa after 1680
cards.def: After 1680 more than 80 percent of new slaves entering the Chesapeake and mainland North America came directly from Africa, mostly Senegal–Niger coast and Angola.

cards.term: How long the Middle Passage lasted and its death rate
cards.def: The Middle Passage lasted three weeks to three months, and historians estimate 15 of every 85 Africans who reached the Americas died during the voyage.

cards.term: How deadly seasoning was in the Chesapeake
cards.def: One-quarter of Africans died in their first year in the Chesapeake, and seasoning mortality in Carolina and the Caribbean was even higher.

cards.term: What share of Virginians were Black by 1740
cards.def: By 1740 40 percent of Virginians were Black, most of them African-born, after direct imports from Africa had surged following 1680.

cards.term: What punishment Virginia law set for a Black person striking a white person
cards.def: Under Virginia's late-seventeenth-century slave laws, a Black person who struck a white person could receive thirty lashes.

cards.term: How much land most small Chesapeake planters held after 1700
cards.def: After 1700 most small Virginia and Maryland planters held 50 to 200 acres and owned no slaves or only two or three.

cards.term: When Barbados turned to sugar
cards.def: In the 1640s Barbados planters learned Dutch sugar-processing methods, and Dutch traders supplied African slaves and marketed the sugar in the Netherlands.

cards.term: How Africans outnumbered English in the Caribbean
cards.def: By the early eighteenth century Africans outnumbered English residents of the Caribbean four to one, and seven major slave uprisings shook the English islands.

cards.term: When the Carolinas were granted to proprietors
cards.def: In 1663 Charles II granted the Carolinas to joint proprietors after William Berkeley and Sir John Colleton persuaded him.

cards.term: When the first permanent South Carolina settlement was founded
cards.def: In 1669 Shaftesbury's English and Barbadian immigrants founded South Carolina's first permanent settlement, and by 1680 Charles Town stood at the Ashley and Cooper Rivers.

cards.term: How many Florida missions Carolina raiders destroyed
cards.def: After Governor James Moore's 1702 attack, Creeks, Yamasees, and Englishmen destroyed 29 Spanish missions, confining Spain to St. Augustine by 1706.

cards.term: How many Indian slaves Carolinians took before 1715
cards.def: Before 1715 Carolinians purchased or captured 30,000 to 50,000 Indian slaves, and South Carolina exported more slaves than it imported.

cards.term: How many white people lived on the South Carolina coast by 1730
cards.def: Malaria, yellow fever, smallpox, and respiratory disease made the swampy coast so deadly that only 10,000 white people lived there by 1730.

cards.term: When Black people became South Carolina's majority
cards.def: Black people became a majority in South Carolina by 1708 and outnumbered whites two to one by 1730.

cards.term: What Georgia's trustees gave settlers
cards.def: Georgia's trustees paid passage and gave 50 acres, tools, and a year of supplies, capped holdings at 500 acres, and banned slavery and hard liquor.

cards.term: What the colony table lists for southern colony populations in 1700
cards.def: The colony table lists about 72,000 in Virginia, 30,000 in Maryland, 65,000 in the British West Indies, 6,000 in South Carolina, and 10,700 in North Carolina in 1700.

cards.term: What the colony table lists for Spanish colonies and Georgia
cards.def: The colony table lists St. Augustine founded 1565 with 1,500 Spaniards by 1700, New Mexico's 2,500 including Indian slaves in 1675, and Georgia's 5,000 in 1752.
